item.title: Nvidia's latest driver update had me thinking my GPU was dead, but this one fix stopped my screen from flickering
item.itunes:title: Nvidia's latest driver update had me thinking my GPU was dead, but this one fix stopped my screen from flickering
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When Nvidia's 616.56 driver landed on my Nvidia App at the end of August, I installed it the way I'd installed every single Game Ready driver, which was, without a second thought. That very same evening after work, I booted Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 like I always do, but after a few minutes of flying, I started seeing strange artefacts across the screen. A few minutes later, the game dropped me on the desktop, ruining over 30-ish minutes of progress.

Like any other paranoid user, I assumed the worst. A little after two years of use, my RTX 4070 Ti Super was done for. A few minutes later, though, I found that it hadn't, and I only worked that out after a fellow XDA colleague reported similar problems on his own machine. That ruled out the dead GPU theory, and pointed straight at the update everyone had just installed. The fix, however, wasn't straightforward. Here's how I got my screen to behave fine again after the latest botched driver update.

A little about the botched Nvidia driver update in question

616.56 created problems that Nvidia refused to ship a hotfix for

Credit: Nvidia.

The problematic driver, as widely reported by the community, is GeForce Game Ready 616.56, which Nvidia pushed out at the end of August. Within a few days, its own feedback thread and subreddits were filled with complaints that ranged from display flickering, artefacting, and in some severe cases, dropping to a black screen. This affected multiple GPUs, from GTX 16 series through RTX 30, 40, and 50-series cards. This was widely reported by a number of news outlets.

The pattern most users landed on pointed at color depth, and the panels set to 8-bit were most affected. In some cases, switching to 10-bit output or turning on Windows Automatic Color Management stopped it, but of course, Nvidia never confirmed this.

Nvidia was quick to take note of the problem, but frustratingly enough, their fix wasn't comprehensive. On September 5, the company shipped a hotfix through 616.86, but it only addressed intermittent browser flickering, broken virtual displays, and black screens in some Remote Desktop sessions. The same fixes were folded into the WQHL 616.92 driver on September 9, but the flickering went untouched in both. So, in some ways, it's still an ongoing issue, which is why it's worth knowing how to fix this.

Nvidia's "absolutely abhorrent" drivers are getting worse, investigation reveals

Best hold off on that driver update for now.

3
By  Jacob Roach

A driver rollback didn't fix the problem for me

If it were that simple, the article wouldn't exist

With the issue identified, the first, and the most obvious thing to do, was to roll the driver back. If 616.56 broke it, an older release should undo the damage. So, naturally, I reverted through the Nvidia App, rebooted, and waited for the flickering to stop.

To my absolute surprise (and sheer horror), it didn't. The problem persisted and the annoying flickering continued on the same apps as though nothing had changed at all. This had my mind going in different directions, such as residual states or perhaps an incomplete cleanup. I also tried switching up the DisplayPort wires to see if it would make a difference, which did not.

This result, however, carried a useful clue. If going back a driver branch did nothing, the fault isn't limited just to the driver. Part of the problem was in the Windows environment itself, in the Desktop Window Manager specifically, and how it hands display surfaces to the panel.

I now stopped tinkering with drivers altogether and started looking for the setting that governed this behavior directly, and it was a single registry value in Windows. This seemed to be the one setting that finally stopped the flickering for good.

I'm so frustrated with Nvidia's drivers, yet things don't look to be getting any better

The entire RTX 40 and RTX 50 series debacle has left me feeling completely fed up.

10
By  Adam Conway

The fix was one registry value

One DWORD in Windows did what a rollback couldn't

The registry workaround to this problem that I was talking about governs something called the Multi-Plane Overlay, or MPO for short. MPO lets the Desktop Window Manager hand certain display surfaces straight to the panel instead of composing them first, and it was this handoff flicking on and off that was producing the flicker. Switching it off came down to a single registry edit, which was the solution that finally worked for me.

If the driver rollback didn't work, it's a solution that could fix your flickering as well. The value you are looking for is called OverlayTestMode. It's a DWORD, set to 5, and it can be found under: 

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Dwm

The fix itself is simple, and can be done in a few minutes. Here is how I did it:

  1. Open the Registry Editor by using the combination Windows + R, type regedit, and hit Enter. On the side of caution, it's best to create a System Restore point first.
  2. Paste the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Dwm into the address bar at the top and press Enter.
  3. Right-click an empty area in the right pane, choose New, followed by DWORD (32-bit) Value, name it exactly OverlayTestMode.
  4. Double-click the new OverlayTestMode file created, enter 5 in the "Value" field, leave the base as Hexadecimal, and click OK.
  5. Restart Windows for the change to take effect.

This change, of course, is fully reversible, so deleting the value puts Windows back exactly as it was. Although it is always recommended to create a System Restore point to make sure there's a hassle-free way to roll back changes in case there are unintended consequences.

When in doubt, check the drivers first

An astonishing number of users online were fully convinced that their GPU or the VRAM chip is dying as a result of this driver update, including myself, until I decided to check the root cause of this issue online. Unfortunately, drivers producing unintended consequences on hardware, even from companies like Nvidia, have become a rather common occurrence, and this one was a textbook case. This is primarily the reason why I'm an advocate for keeping frequent system restore points, and where possible, maintaining a log of important changes to your PC.

item.title: I ditched Pocket for Karakeep, and my research library finally became searchable
item.itunes:title: I ditched Pocket for Karakeep, and my research library finally became searchable
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Researching and saving things is a pretty standard part of my workflow. Be it articles I want to read, tutorials for projects, just interesting projects and software to write about, and more. For a long time, my workflow revolved around Pocket. But with Pocket no longer a thing, I've tried to look up a proper alternative. I even tried using bookmarks, but that got out of hand pretty quickly.

So I started looking for an app that took Pocket's approach to saving daily reads and data, without the costs attached. I needed something searchable, with the ability to keep long-term archives. That's how I landed on Karakeep. Installed via Docker on my home server, it's become the place where I throw practically anything I find interesting. It's given me a way to build a searchable personal library out of the things I read practically every day.

Shiori is the best self-hosted bookmark manager I didn't know I needed

Win the fight against link rot by self-hosting your own bookmark service.

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Ditch the tab clutter

Offline archives sold me on Karakeep

Credit: 

I know there are a lot of Karakeep pros out there, but my biggest use case is honestly the simplest. Anytime I come across something interesting that I want to catch up with later, I save it to Karakeep instead of leaving the tab open or adding another bookmark to my browser. I've got the Chrome bookmark installed, and it makes this step basically a one-tap affair.

Unlike a basic bookmark, Karakeep pulls in a fair degree of relevant information from the page. For example, it can store the title, description, and previews. Internet information is ephemeral, and I like holding on to archival copies of interesting reads for posterity, so I've even enabled the archival features. This means that any time I save a web page, Karakeep pulls down a full copy that I can read offline.

This last feature is what truly sold me on Karakeep. It's not the only bookmarking service with archival features, but I don't want to trust cloud services with a backup. Certainly not as the only copy. Websites disappear, URLs change, and articles might even get updated. All too often, I've tapped a bookmark from a decade ago for a cool nugget of information, only to find that the website doesn't exist anymore. It makes me sad.

Karakeep can retain an archived version of the page that gives me usable data even when the original website goes down.

Karakeep has become my personal research library

It saves more than web pages

While my initial goal was to find a bookmarking service, I've found that Karakeep serves a few additional use cases for me. I've started using it to save reference PDFs, images, or even text fragments. Karakeep treats links, text, and media as different types of bookmarks, so it serves as a one-stop shop for saving different kinds of material.

I tend to read a lot of research papers, so this combined system works particularly well for me. Plus, if the paper is relevant to an article I've been researching, I now have a single source of information for all my research. I tie all these disparate pieces using a system of tags, which helps me filter out information easily.

That said, Karakeep also offers full-text search across all the piecesyou've been saving, so it's never too hard to find what you're looking for. In fact, unlike some bookmarking services that stick to searchable page titles and URLs, the ability to search an archive means that you can effectively search by using whatever you remember of an article instead of trying to remember keywords.

While I prefer to handle tagging manually, like most software today, Karakeep too offers AI integration if you want it. You can connect to a range of AI service providers to auto-suggest and populate tags, which gives you another way to sort through your collection of bookmarks.

On the topic of curation, there's plenty more to discover here. Take, for example, lists. You can use them in a few different ways. Be it as a running reading-it-later list, or a collection of related lists. You can even set up a smart list that auto-updates based on tags. There's a lot of flexibility here. Similarly, like a half-decent PDF reader or even a Kindle, you can highlight sections of a long read. These highlights are also individually searchable, but more than that, when it's time to review a document, you can see the highlighted text right next to it. This has saved me more time than I care to count.

Finally, yes, there are mobile apps too, so you can continue reading and highlighting on-the-go. But that goes without saying.

Much more than just a Pocket replacement

While I was initially looking for a Pocket replacement, Karakeep is so much more than that. It lets you effectively build a local repository of information from across the internet. Be it online articles or offline PDFs, images, and even personal texts. Depending on your use case, you could even consider it a lighter version of Paperless-NGX.

All that said, for something that was really just a simple replacement for a bookmarking app, I've found a surprising amount of utility from Karakeep.

Karakeep

Karakeep is an open-source, self-hosted bookmarks manager that allows you to add bookmarks from any platform and categorizes them based on tags.

item.itunes:title: Microsoft confirms that Windows 11's new update breaks copy-pasting in Excel, and there's no solution yet
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • The latest KB5002914 patch for Windows 11 makes copy-pasting fail silently in Excel 2016–2024.
  • Microsoft is investigating; paste shows no error, and there's currently no workaround.
  • No temporary fix for now; consider trying LibreOffice Calc until Microsoft patches it.

Another Patch Tuesday has come and gone, so you know what that means: more weird Windows 11 bugs. We've already seen the latest patch break WSL and Claude Cowork functionality due to issues with Plan9. Now, Microsoft has confirmed that anyone who downloaded the latest update may have issues copy-pasting in Excel.

The latest Patch Tuesday update is breaking copy-paste functionality in Excel

Worst of all, it won't even tell you what's wrong

As spotted by Neowin, Microsoft has confirmed a new bug for Excel in its description of the KB5002914 September patch. As it turns out, if you've been trying to copy-paste data in Excel and it seemingly doesn't work despite you ensuring you did everything correctly, it's not just you:

In Microsoft Excel 2024, 2021, 2019, and 2016, the paste operation might fail silently. Although users try to paste content, the source remains selected and the destination is unmodified. When this issue occurs, users receive no indication of the failure, such as a beep or error message. Microsoft is researching the issue and will post more information in this article when the information becomes available.

The good news is that it's the only known bug in Excel introduced with KB5002914. The bad news is that it's a very annoying bug, and there's nothing we can do to temporarily fix it on our end while Microsoft works on a patch. I guess we'll just have to sit tight and wait for Microsoft to get a patch out. On the other hand, this might be the perfect excuse to give LibreOffice Calc a try.

item.title: I found where Windows keeps files you deleted years ago, and it wasn't the Recycle Bin
item.itunes:title: I found where Windows keeps files you deleted years ago, and it wasn't the Recycle Bin
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every Windows user on the planet has been familiar with the Recycle Bin for years now. Its name itself has led me to believe that it's the final stop for anything I delete from Windows. By and large, I've always assumed that emptying the Recycle Bin meant that the files were gone, with the only exception being specialized recovery software.

That assumption fell apart when I stumbled across a Windows folder that contained remnants of files I had deleted months and even years ago.

Admittedly, I was caught just a little off guard by how ordinary this mechanism was, and how my old data had survived this long. Naturally, this sent me down a rabbit hole as I dug through my PC to figure out exactly what Windows was hoarding, why it was still there, and if those leftovers were any use at all.

I deleted system32 so you don't have to, and here's what actually happened

What happens if you delete System32? I did it and the outcome wasn't pleasant.

41
By  Brian Burgess

Windows doesn't forget as easily as you might think

The Recycle Bin is only one layer

The first clue I found was when I went looking for a bunch of screenshots I had deleted during a cleanup. I right-clicked the Screenshots folder, opened Properties, and noticed the Previous Versions tab. Truth be told, I wasn't expecting much, but one of the older versions opened into a familiar folder structure. Lo and behold, it also had my deleted files sitting exactly where I left them — Windows had apparently decided that deleting something didn't necessarily mean saying goodbye.

That is essentially what shadow copies can do. Windows can preserve earlier states of files and folders, allowing Previous Versions to show what existed before you deleted something. Since the relevant snapshot still existed, I restored the file with remarkably little friction. Plus, I didn't even have to install any recovery software like DiskDrill, since I just effectively asked Windows to hand me an older copy of reality.

The Previous Versions feature uses Windows' Volume Shadow Copy Service (or File History and System Restore Points) in order to snapshot file system states. Checking the previous version of a folder can bring back files deleted after that snapshot was initially created.

Shadow copies are created during system restore points, Windows Updates, or scheduled tasks — they do not take real-time snapshots of every file change.

There's also a cache that refuses to forget anything

Windows keeps the picture but not the file itself

Windows also holds a thumbnail cache of hundreds, if not thousands, of files. These are stored as thumbcache_*.db files on the PC, but you can't easily view them all. Viewing them requires software like Thumbcache Viewer to open the internal database files. What I found were recognizable images from files I had deleted months and years ago. The thumbnail cache showed me old photos, screenshots, and document pages — even highly sensitive ones — all still there.

Now, it's not like Windows had preserved the original files themselves. What it had retained were representations generated for Explorer. For a photo, however, the difference is almost academic. A thumbnail can still reveal faces in photographs and screenshots.

The thumbnail cache, when viewed with Thumbcache Viewer, showed me old photos I thought I'd deleted — even highly sensitive ones.

The privacy problem felt difficult to ignore. It took me seconds to identify files I knew were gone, simply by looking at their previews. I blurred personal content in my screenshot, so if a thumbnail is enough to recognize something sensitive, there felt little point in "deleting" certain files.

The cache isn't the only historian on Windows, either. Jump Lists and Recent Items can retain filenames and paths for files that no longer exist. They don't contain the original data, but preserve a breadcrumb trail. Unlike temporary leftovers, these records can survive years.

Windows has too many backup tools, but this free app beats them all

I stopped trusting Windows backups after learning what actually works

1
By  Ayush Pande

Deleting a file is only the beginning

The apps have their own version of "gone"

By this point, I was wondering how many places on my PC had decided that my deleted files deserved a second life. The answer got more annoying when I stopped looking at Windows itself. Apparently, OneDrive has its own Recycle Bin, and it's not alone, either. Plenty of other apps maintain their own trash, recovery, or cache folders. Deleting something inside an app doesn't necessarily mean that Windows gets the final say.

So I did the boring thing that turned out to be productive — I started cleaning. Windows 11's Storage Sense can automate some housekeeping, while Disk Cleanup let me dig deeper by selecting system files and clearing things such as Windows.old and cached thumbnails. I also checked which apps had accumulated debris and emptied the obvious bins.

My cleanup recovered roughly 20GB. That was the useful part of this rabbit hole — the same leftovers that can rescue a deleted file can also be needlessly occupying valuable space on the SSD.

It was free and saved me from buying a new SSD.

20
By  Jasmine Mannan

Deleting something really shouldn't require a forensic investigation

Windows clearly has a habit of keeping its leftovers around. A PC is a constantly-changing system that makes trade-offs on your behalf, often prioritizing convenience, recovery, and performance over the satisfying finality of a Delete key.

Regardless, I don't plan on treating every cache on my PC as a privacy emergency. This data (or most of it, at least) exists for mundane reasons, and much of it also disappears eventually. Now when I delete something, I don't assume the operating system has forgotten it. I know better, and the extra bit of skepticism that Windows justifiably warrants is precisely what makes my PC easier to manage.

item.title: I asked Claude Code, Codex, and Google Antigravity to rebuild the same website; one is in a different league
item.itunes:title: I asked Claude Code, Codex, and Google Antigravity to rebuild the same website; one is in a different league
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
AI coding tools are getting quite good at building websites, but I wanted to know which current model can nail all the little details that I ask for in a prompt. So I gave Claude Code, Codex, and Google Antigravity the exact same challenge: rebuild a website from the same brief, with no extra hand-holding along the way.

On paper, all three should have produced something polished. In practice, the results were nowhere near as close as I expected.

I gave Claude Code and Google Antigravity a full project, and they finished twice as fast as VS Code alone

VS Code needs to catch up.

15
By  Anurag Singh

A word about the prompt

And my preferred coding models

To keep this comparison as fair as possible, I am sticking with the default flagship coding agents available in each tool: Opus 5 in Claude Code, GPT-5.6 in Codex, and Gemini 3.8 in Google Antigravity. I am also giving all three the exact same prompt, with no extra hints or follow-up instructions during the first run.

This isn't a simple one-page portfolio test either. I picked a fairly complex food-delivery website with a dedicated hero section, restaurant filters, responsive layouts, animations, testimonials, and multiple interactive elements.

The prompt also asks each agent to make its own design decisions from scratch, so this test should reveal which tool turns a demanding brief into a polished website.

Google Antigravity

Gemini finally feels seriously competitive

Google clearly wasn’t kidding when it talked up the coding improvements in Gemini 3.8. I have used Gemini 3.5 inside Antigravity before, and the difference here is impressive.

The first thing that impressed me was the overall presentation. The generated food imagery looked good, the animations were smooth, without being distracting, and Gemini did a great job of giving different sections their own personality instead of turning the entire page into the usual collection of white cards.

I especially liked the offer and newsletter sections, where it used a dark gradient treatment that instantly made them stand out from the rest of the page. Those sections looked like something a designer had spent time refining rather than a generic AI-generated layout.

It wasn’t flawless, though. The FAQ section felt cramped. The mobile mockups were even worse. They looked laughably artificial compared to the rest of the site.

Still, these are minor misses. The overall output is excellent, and Antigravity generated everything at blazing-fast speed. It doesn’t quite take the crown, but it easily earns second place.

ChatGPT Codex

It looks polished until closer inspection

Codex made a strong first impression. The website looked clean, the layout was sensible, and GPT-5.6 followed my prompt closely without leaving out any of the major sections. The animations were decent, the food imagery worked well, and everything felt functional right from the first run.

The hero section was easily the highlight for me. In fact, I would say it was the best hero design out of all three tools. It used a large food image effectively, and layered in small floating details such as ratings, delivery information, and short taglines around it.

The problems started showing up once I looked more closely. Typography continues to be one of my biggest complaints with GPT-5.6 when I use it for website design. The fonts were small in several areas, like secondary text and supporting copy.

This is something I have noticed with GPT-5.6-generated interfaces, and I usually end up asking it to increase font sizes. The newsletter section was another weak point. It felt rushed, plain, and unfinished.

That sums up my experience with Codex here. It did almost everything I asked, and there were no major disasters. But it lacked the final layer of refinement that separates a good AI-generated website from one that looks professionally designed.

I tried Cursor’s top alternatives after Elon Musk’s SpaceX agreed to buy it, and I have a clear winner for you

The AI coding race just changed

11
By  Parth Shah

Claude Code

It wins on tiny details

Claude Code was the one that felt the most complete from the start. It wasn’t just that the website worked or that it followed my prompt properly. What stood out was how well it handled all the small design decisions that usually need another round of cleanup.

The typography felt right, the spacing was consistent, the padding around cards and sections was properly judged, and the image placement looked intentional.

The mobile mockups were impressive. This is one area where both GPT-5.6 and Gemini fall apart, but Claude Code got them almost spot on. They actually looked like believable app interfaces instead of generic phone frames with random content stuffed inside.

The live tracking detail made the whole experience feel much closer to a real food-delivery product. It was one of those small touches that leaves a strong impression in front of your client. Claude didn’t make any of the mistakes that I found with Gemini and GPT. The consistency carried across the entire page, which is what impressed me most.

If I had to nitpick, I still preferred Codex’s hero section. Claude Code’s version was good, but it didn’t have quite the same visual impact or those clever floating details around the main image. However, once I looked at the website as a whole, Claude Code was the obvious winner.

Three agents entered, one dominated

After putting all three through the exact same challenge, Claude Code came out on top for me. Antigravity was the biggest surprise and easily earned second place, while Codex impressed me with its hero section but fell short on overall polish.

What separated Claude Code was consistency. The typography, spacing, mockups, tracking section, FAQ, and newsletter all felt finished.

item.title: Your TV is adding motion smoothing to everything, and switching it off isn't the whole fix
item.itunes:title: Your TV is adding motion smoothing to everything, and switching it off isn't the whole fix
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For a long time, Hollywood waged a crusade against motion smoothing, with directors and actors begging consumers to dig into their TV settings and kill Auto Motion, Auto Motion Plus, or Motion Flow to eradicate the sickening hyperreal soap opera effect.

Even if you toggle motion smoothing off on your high-end OLED TV, you might still see wide panning shots across landscapes or city skylines look agonizingly harsh, with choppy, jarring, flickering that feels like an aggressive strobe light. It feels worse than the soap opera effect you just killed.

Turning off motion smoothing only solves half the problem. Modern OLED panels have near-instantaneous pixel response times, which turn the natural 24fps film cadence into aggressive motion stutter. To get genuine cinematic motion without the soap effect, you have to understand the physical difference between judder and stutter.

Understanding stutter vs judder

You need to know the difference

Stutter and judder are different. Modern TVs don't flicker like old CRT tubes or 35mm film projectors with spinning shutters. They're sample-and-hold displays. This means an image frame is held completely static and illuminated on screen until the next refresh cycle draws the next frame.

Vintage LCDs essentially hide 24p judder because of slow pixel response. Older LCD TVs have slow pixel response times of 10ms to 30ms, which means pixels physically took time to transition from gray to gray, creating natural hardware-level motion blur that smoothed the visual jump between 24 fps frames.

With OLED, you get sub-millisecond response time, which can lead to severe stutter. OLED pixels transition states at under 0.1ms. At 24fps each frame stays frozen on screen for roughly 41.4ms, completely razor-sharp, before instantly teleporting to the next frame position. Your eye tracks the motion smoothly across the screen, but the image holds still and then leaps. The result is stutter: a perceived stroboscopic slideshow during slow pans.

Judder is something different entirely and is instead a mathematical timing error. When a 24fps film is broadcast over a standard 60 Hz video signal, like with cable boxes or standard streaming sticks, 24 does not divide evenly into 60. This means the TV alternates between showing one film frame for two refreshes and the next for three refreshes, leading to 3:2 pull-down. This creates an uneven limping cadence, completely distinct from OLED stutter.

Why does turning off motion smoothing not solve the problem?

There are other issues to consider

When it comes to motion smoothing, turning the feature off and simply leaving it can lead you to motion purgatory. Many streaming boxes, like Roku, Chromecast with Google TV, or even older Firesticks, output a fixed 60 Hz HDMI signal by default. Even if your TV has a native 120Hz panel capable of a 5x pull-down (repeating every 24 fps frame exactly 5 times), it can't reconstruct the 24p cadence if the streaming stick baked a 3x2 pull-down into the signal before it reached the HDMI port.

Built-in TV apps like WebOS, Tizen, Google TV, or Netflix can often bypass HDMI timing issues, but they secretly re-engage vendor post-processing profiles under HDR and Dolby Vision modes even if you disable them in SDR. Variable refresh rate, or VRR, can also lead to conflicts. Leaving game mode or ALLM enabled for media consumption disables the TV's cadence reconstruction algorithms entirely, forcing 60Hz pull-down judder directly onto movies.

How can you solve the problem?

There are some settings you can adjust

So what is the real solution? The best option is to actually turn on Filmmaker Mode. The setting name depends on your TV brand. With LG TVs, it's sometimes called Real Cinema Mode, and it forces a 5x5 pull-down on 120Hz panels. On Sony TVs, it's often called Motion Flow, set to Custom, with CineMotion set to High. On Samsung TVs, you can adjust Picture Clarity to Custom, then set Film Mode to Auto. These features are designed to extract 24p from 60p/60i signals, so they should hopefully fix the judder for you.

The UHD Alliance introduced these filmmaker modes to automatically disable smoothing, correct color temperatures to D65, and lock the native aspect ratio with a single metadata flag.

But the missing piece is that filmmaker mode correctly turns on aggressive MEMC interpolation, but it does nothing to fix OLED sample-and-hold stutter. For viewers, it's still sensitive to OLED strobe and bus-kick pans, and standard filmmaker mode will leave them right back in the starter trap unless they manually customize their motion submenu.

You can do this by adjusting your interpolation settings. Don't just leave it on a binary on/off toggle. Instead, switch to custom/user mode, set de-blur to 0 or low because it's not needed for 24p, and set de-judder to 1 or 2, which is typically out of 10.

Motion smoothing isn't great

But you have to understand the alternative

The battle against motion smoothing was 100% justified, but the advice given to consumers was seemingly too simplistic. Blindly turning off every motion setting on a modern OLED ignores the physics of sub-millisecond pixel response times and sample-and-hold display technology. Stop toggling motion smoothing between two extremes.

By enabling filmmaker mode and manually customizing your interpolation, you can enjoy your movies the way the directors graded them in the studio and hopefully avoid both judder and stutter.

item.title: I replaced Photoshop, Illustrator, and InDesign with three free apps, and only one felt like a downgrade
item.itunes:title: I replaced Photoshop, Illustrator, and InDesign with three free apps, and only one felt like a downgrade
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Giving up an Adobe subscription used to mean settling for less or accepting some type of compromise somewhere. Perhaps the free replacements had the features but not the polish, or perhaps it was reliable but so ugly that you dreaded opening it. So recommending free alternatives always came with a bunch of caveats, and sometimes still does.

That's less true now than it even was a year ago. Being Adobe-free has become almost a skill for me at this point, having tested what feels like hundreds of alternatives. But at the end of the day, some tools are simply better than others, depending on your workflow and the features you're after specifically…

I replaced Adobe, Figma, and Canva with one free tool, and I'm not paying for design software again

It's an all-kill design tool

15
By  Nolen Jonker

The free creative tool space looks different than it did two years ago

2025 was a complete reset

A couple of years ago, recommending free Adobe alternatives usually meant sending someone to GIMP, Inkscape, and Scribus, and every one of those came with a "but" attached. They still have that clunky vibe to their interfaces and missing features, take your pick. Then in October 2025, Canva took the three Affinity apps that used to cost around $70 each (Designer, Photo, Publisher) and turned them into one free app called Affinity. This pretty much ended the question of which free tool can replace Adobe overnight, and I still think this is one of the biggest moves in terms of accessibility in the design space.

But Affinity isn't the only thing that changed. Penpot hit its 2.0 release with a full UI overhaul and native design tokens, and it's now a legit Figma alternative with self-hosting for teams that care about data ownership. Even the older open-source tools have picked up AI features through community extensions, though that's a slower burn than the Affinity thing.

What this all comes down to is that the question in 2026 and onward isn't what you're giving up anymore, it's about what you're gaining when building a new creative stack.

I replaced Adobe, Figma, and Canva with ChatGPT and one open-source tool

Girl math says this counts as three cancelled subscriptions

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

The two free apps doing all the heavy lifting

One handles three Adobe apps by itself, the other is for browser-based convenience

Photopea was my go-to Photoshop alternative back when I still had a Photoshop subscription. Sometimes I'd have Photoshop open and still switch to Photopea for something quick, or just to see how both compare on the same task or which is faster. It's entirely browser-based, meaning I can even run it smoothly on my Chromebook, and completely designed to feel like Photoshop, so pretty much every part of the interface maps to something you already know.

It also opens PSD files properly, not the way GIMP does where layers sometimes come in flattened or with effects stripped. The non-destructive workflow is also solid - even though Affinity is free now, I find Photopea's adjustments and masking a little more intuitive, so I still use it for quick edits because loading up a browser tab is faster than a desktop app.

Speaking of Affinity, that's pretty much where the rest happens because it now does the work of Photoshop, Illustrator, and InDesign completely free in the unified app, via its three workspaces Pixel, Vector, and Layout. The pen tool in Vector has a proper Smart mode that auto-generates smooth curves as you draw, which sounds minor but saves a genuinely annoying amount of node cleanup work. Boolean operations work non-destructively if you hold Alt when you click them, which is a lifesaver for icon work where I might want to revisit the compound shape later.

The Layout workspace covers what InDesign did, with full CMYK and everything else you'd need for actual print work. What ties it all together is StudioLink, which lets me switch between workspaces without leaving the document. Say I'm doing a layout and want to retouch a placed image, I click into Pixel, make the edit, and the layout updates in real time.

The only caveat here is that you need a Canva account to use Affinity now, but a free one is fine, there's no subscription requirement unless you want Canva's AI features.

All in all, Photopea is still pretty much my go-to when it comes to Photoshop replacements, with Affinity Pixel being a close second. But I've actually come to prefer Affinity's Vector workspace as an Illustrator alternative over anything else. And I've never had much use for InDesign, but Layout is there too should I need it.

This free Photoshop alternative does what GIMP and Krita can't, and I stopped looking after trying it

Lightweight, free, and powerful.

1
By  Parth Shah

Inkscape felt like a downgrade

It's not bad, I just have something that's already better

I still have Inkscape on my PC and run it from time to time, but honestly since Affinity became free, I haven't found myself reaching for Inkscape as much at all, simply because having a vector editor that's inside the app I'm already using for raster graphics is more convenient.

Inkscape is a genuinely capable vector editor, with the benefit of being open-source too and an active community behind it. Plus it has cross-platform support that includes Linux (which Affinity doesn't do natively). But when I actually sat down to figure out my Adobe replacement stack, Inkscape kept losing to Affinity. Beyond the workspace convenience, Affinity also has a more intuitive UI, with Inkscape still retaining a bit of that clunky open-source feel to it.

This open-source tool combines Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and After Effects - And it replaced all three for me

I didn't expect it to replace my entire Adobe setup

13
By  Nolen Jonker

The Adobe alternative conversation has shifted

If you'd told me a few years ago that I'd be replacing a multi-hundred-dollar-a-year Adobe subscription with a browser tab and one free desktop app, I wouldn't have believed it. But this is the state of free design software right now, and I'm not complaining one bit. Sure, the stack isn't fully open-source, but the work gets done either way because my options aren't limited to eccentric and complicated interfaces of niche alternatives anymore.

item.title: Samsung's $4.99 SmartThings fee follows you to Home Assistant
item.itunes:title: Samsung's $4.99 SmartThings fee follows you to Home Assistant
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For about a month now, a smart plug and a starter hub have been sitting in my browser tab. The plan was to control a lamp, monitor two doors, and keep everything running while I’m away. I chose Home Assistant for it, and then Samsung said it would start charging $4.99 a month for the SmartThings API.

This fee is to begin in October, so I started finding workarounds. I traced how a command actually gets from a dashboard to a lamp. It turns outmany smart home problems need a different solution than we think. And if you are a smart home enthusiast like me, you need to know this. Let's begin.

I wouldn't build another smart home without Zigbee, even with Matter everywhere

Cheaper, more stable and gives you access to all of the features.

3
By  Jasmine Mannan

Your light switch mails a letter to Samsung's servers

And Samsung has decided to charge postage

Home Assistant tags every integration with something it calls an IoT class. The SmartThings one is marked Cloud Push, and this label is the whole story.

Consider that your dashboard is in your living room and your lamp is eight feet away. Now, when you tap the button, the instructions leave your house and go to Samsung's servers. From there, it updates the exact command for your lamp and comes back to your dashboard.

For years, that letter traveled free. On June 23, Samsung announced it is moving the SmartThings API to paid tiers, including a $4.99 monthly personal plan for individual developers. Free access runs through the end of September. From October, the postage is yours.

That works out to about $60 a year to send letters between devices inside your own house.

The fee is not charged for the SmartThings app. It is for programmatic access that talks to Samsung's servers for you.

The mailbox key used to last 50 years, and now it expires overnight

Read the screenshot; it's not a typo

Before any of this, a Personal Access Token was the easy way in. You generated one, pasted it into whatever you were building, and it worked. Samsung's own authorization docs still record what happened next. A token created before December 30, 2024, could be set to last up to 50 years. A token created after that date is valid for 24 hours.

Fifty years to one day, on the same page, one sentence apart. I read it twice because the numbers look like a typo. They are not. Anyone running a home-brewed script after that date had to re-key it every morning or rebuild around OAuth. Most people quietly stopped.

So October is the last bolt on a door that started closing eighteen months ago. Samsung's developer terms, meanwhile, have always said the company can revise them at any time without notice. Nobody reads the back of the envelope. Which left the only question that mattered to my cart, and we are at it now.

How to tell if a smart home device needs Samsung's cloud before you buy it

The check takes a minute, and it is free

Every Home Assistant integration page carries its IoT class on a small card at the bottom. Local Push and Local Polling mean the traffic stays inside your house. Cloud Push and Cloud Polling mean it does not.

So now, before I buy anything, I search for the brand on the Home Assistant integrations page and scroll to that line. That is the whole test. SmartThings reads Cloud Push. Zigbee Home Automation reads Local Push. Those two words separate a device that keeps working when your internet drops from one that stops.

The scale caught me off guard. That same card puts the SmartThings integration at 10.2% of active installations that report usage, about one in ten. Reporting is opt-in, so the true figure sits higher. It is not about owning, though, but renting. Samsung's rate limit page caps the Device APIs at 12 requests per minute per device.

Open home-assistant.io/integrations, search for the brand, and scroll to the card at the bottom of its page. Local means your commands stay home. Cloud means they take a trip.

Zigbee and Z-Wave devices skip Samsung's servers entirely, and a $30 Zigbee dongle is all you need to host that network yourself.

At $4.99 a month, the Zigbee dongle pays for itself

This could make your shopping list easy.

So I already own a Samsung fridge, a Samsung washer, and a Samsung TV. Sadly, none of the above rescues me in this case.

Matter was supposed to be the fix. In practice, Samsung's Matter-capable appliances cannot be commissioned into Home Assistant directly. SmartThings stays with the Matter controller, which keeps Samsung's cloud as the only road in. The fridge is not going to learn a second language.

The community is having a go at it. A custom integration called LocalThings reaches newer Samsung appliances over your own network with no cloud round trip. It works, and it wants firmware from roughly 2022 or later. Its own documentation admits the appliance keeps talking to Samsung anyway, because that is firmware behavior with no integration controls.

Leaving is not free either. You cannot reuse the radios inside a SmartThings hub. Every Zigbee device has to be factory reset and paired again, one at a time, and every Z-Wave device excluded, then included. At 30 devices, that is your weekend.

What you own

Can it leave

What it costs you

Zigbee sensors and bulbs

Yes

A USB coordinator, plus a factory reset and re-pair for each device

Z-Wave locks and switches

Yes

A USB coordinator, plus an exclude and include for each device

Matter devices from other brands

Yes

A share code from the SmartThings app, no reset needed

Samsung fridge, washer, or TV

Not really

$4.99 a month, or a community integration and 2022 firmware

Measured against a weekend of resets, $4.99 a month is a fair trade for plenty of people, and I would take it because of those Samsung appliances I already have in my house.

People never really own cloud-powered products

Paulus Schoutsen, who founded Home Assistant, called this yet another cloud paywall, filing it under a running series about how people never really own cloud-powered products. Nobody's device stopped working here. The road it travels grew a tollbooth, and that road was never printed on the box.

item.title: Every SSD has a hidden fast lane, and running out of it is why big file copies crawl
item.itunes:title: Every SSD has a hidden fast lane, and running out of it is why big file copies crawl
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
We love buying our SSDs with the big four-digit megabytes-per-second stickers on the packaging, and it's even more rewarding when CrystalDiskInfo shows the same numbers on the desktop. And yet, way too many times, copying or transferring a large folder sometimes starts off like a rocket ship only to end up like a hard drive transfer from 2010.

Sure, benchmark numbers are always optimistic, and thus unrealistic in day-to-day usage in the real world, but there's more to it than just the numbers — our SSDs do something behind the scenes that we rarely get to see, if ever.

During any big transfer, there comes a point where the drive slows down to a crawl (especially compared to its initial transfer speeds). As such, perhaps the most surprising part about all this is that it isn't necessarily a fault with the drive or with the PC. Instead, the reason lies in how modern NAND is used.

Your SSD is getting slower every month, and there's a built-in fix most people don't know

The TRIM command helps your SSD deliver maximum performance

26
By  Tanveer Singh

There are parts of your SSD you never see

NAND has a clever shortcut for data transfers

NAND flash, which is present on every SSD, stores data by assigning electrical charge to each cell. SLC stores one bit, while TLC and QLC store three and four bits, respectively. More bits create more voltage states to distinguish, making writes slower. The denser cells win when it comes to capacity, but they come with a bit of a programming penalty.

Packing three or four bits into a cell means placing the charge into one of eight or sixteen narrow voltage windows, which the controller can't hit in a single shot. As such, it has to write in multiple passes, nudging the charge closer to the target. This verify-and-adjust cycle works reliably, but it always takes time.

SLC, TLC, and QLC stand for Single-Level Cell, Triple-Level cell, and Quad-Level Cell, respectively. They define the density of NAND flash memory on an SSD.

This penalty doesn't apply to Single-Level Cells, though. SSD controllers work around the time penalty of TLC or QLC by temporarily using part of the NAND as SLC. The cells are still physically the same, but the controller uses fewer states when using SLC. What this achieves is making incoming writes quicker than writing directly into TLC or QLC (depending on which type of cell an SSD uses).

This is how the SLC write cache on an SSD helps the on-board SSD controller transfer files faster. Some drives reserve a fixed portion for this cache, while others let it use available NAND dynamically. Unlike DRAM on an SSD (when a drive ships with DRAM), which mainly helps the controller track where the data is located, the SLC cache holds newly-written data. DRAM may help the drive find information, while the SLC write cache gives incoming writes somewhere faster to land.

I'm done buying DRAM-less SSDs after testing one in my daily PC

Modern DRAM-less SSDs are good, but I'd still pay for DRAM.

4
By  Abid Ahsan Shanto

The fast part runs out, though

That's what causes the sudden speed drops

The impressive sequential-write numbers that SSDs boast about are the easiest to achieve while there is room for the controller to accept incoming data quickly. However, if you keep throwing a sufficiently large transfer at it, that temporary buffer will eventually fill up, at which point, the drive will have to program incoming data into its underlying TLC or QLC arrangement instead.

item.title: I treat my terminal less like a shell and more like a dashboard for everything I have running
item.itunes:title: I treat my terminal less like a shell and more like a dashboard for everything I have running
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I got a MacBook last year and, as I started using it more for work, Terminal quickly became one of those apps I rarely closed. I initially used it the usual way — type a command, get the result, and move on. But macOS is constantly doing things in the background, and checking on the machine usually means digging through separate apps or opening yet another Terminal tab.

These days, I leave one Terminal window set up as a live view of the machine. I can glance at it, understand what the Mac is doing, and deal with anything that looks wrong from the same place. The terminal still works as a shell, of course, but I now spend almost as much time reading it as typing into it.

I built the dashboard around tmux and btop

Tmux is what makes this setup work

Tmux is what makes this setup work. It’s a terminal multiplexer, which means it can hold several terminals inside a single persistent session. You can divide that session into windows and panes, leave commands running inside them, and return later without rebuilding the entire layout.

I paired it with btop, an interactive system monitor that presents macOS information in a much cleaner format than the built-in top command. Both tools are available through Homebrew, so installing the basic setup takes one command.

brew install tmux btop

Btop takes over the terminal and gives you a live view of the Mac. The upper half shows how the CPU and memory are being used, while the lower section covers storage, network activity, and individual processes. You can sort the process list, search for a specific app, switch to a tree view, or select a process and terminate it from the same interface. It’s much easier to scan than a wall of output from top, especially when you only want to know why the Mac is suddenly using more memory or sending data over the network.

I keep btop in its own tmux window because the graphs need room. Tmux uses Ctrl+B as its command prefix, so pressing Ctrl + B followed by C creates another window. You can then press Ctrl + B followed by a number to jump between windows, or use N and P to move to the next or previous one.

The terminal also shows what my services are doing

Including Docker and other tools

I also use Terminal as a dashboard to see how the services that I have running locally on my device are doing. Docker Desktop is a good example. Its menu bar icon tells me that Docker itself is open, but I don’t know whether Jellyfin is working. I can use btop to see if Docker is consuming resources, but it doesn’t explain which container is responsible. To get around this, I keep a tmux window where I move between the container list and live resource usage.

docker ps
docker stats

Docker ps shows whether the Jellyfin container is running, while docker stats shows how much CPU, memory, and network bandwidth it is using. If Jellyfin isn’t responding properly, I can follow its logs from the same window.

docker logs --follow jellyfin

I use Ollama to run LLMs locally, and sometimes it continues serving a model after I have moved on to something else. The model remains loaded in memory until Ollama unloads it or I stop it myself. You can run ollama ps to see which models are currently loaded, and ollama stop followed by the model name removes one that you no longer need.

I connect to my homelab through Tailscale and keep an SSH session available in another window. tailscale status confirms that the Mac can reach the homelab before I connect. Nextcloud and Immich run on that machine, so once I’m inside, I can use the same Docker commands to check their containers, read their logs, or restart a service.

The terminal can replace more GUI apps than you think

There's a terminal alternative for almost every app

A lot of people open Terminal only when a tutorial tells them to paste a command into it. Modern terminal apps are far more approachable than that. Many have full-screen interfaces, mouse support, file previews, menus, and keyboard shortcuts, so you don’t need to memorize dozens of commands before they become useful.

Yazi is one of the best examples. It’s a fast file manager with a three-pane layout that shows the parent directory, the current folder, and a preview of the selected file. It can preview images, PDFs, archives, videos, and code without opening another app. I can move around the filesystem and manage files without constantly switching between the keyboard and trackpad, which is one of the reasons I prefer it to most graphical file managers.

Even web browsing works from the command line. Lynx and w3m strip websites down to their text and links, which makes them useful for reading documentation, articles, and other text-heavy pages.

There are plenty of more specialized tools as well. For example, ncdu gives you an interactive view of disk usage and makes it easy to find oversized directories. Lazygit can turn Git branches, commits, diffs, and staging into a keyboard-driven interface without requiring a heavyweight desktop client. And Neovim can replace a graphical text editor once you add the plugins you need.

Terminal is not as intimidating as it seems

Terminal has a reputation for being difficult because it greets you with a blank window and no obvious place to start. But you don’t need to learn the entire command line before you can use it. You can just start with a tool that does something useful, look up the few commands you need, and pick up the rest over time.

There's a terminal alternative for almost every app

A lot of people open Terminal only when a tutorial tells them to paste a command into it. Modern terminal apps are far more approachable than that. Many have full-screen interfaces, mouse support, file previews, menus, and keyboard shortcuts, so you don’t need to memorize dozens of commands before they become useful.

Yazi is one of the best examples. It’s a fast file manager with a three-pane layout that shows the parent directory, the current folder, and a preview of the selected file. It can preview images, PDFs, archives, videos, and code without opening another app. I can move around the filesystem and manage files without constantly switching between the keyboard and trackpad, which is one of the reasons I prefer it to most graphical file managers.

Even web browsing works from the command line. Lynx and w3m strip websites down to their text and links, which makes them useful for reading documentation, articles, and other text-heavy pages.

There are plenty of more specialized tools as well. For example, ncdu gives you an interactive view of disk usage and makes it easy to find oversized directories. Lazygit can turn Git branches, commits, diffs, and staging into a keyboard-driven interface without requiring a heavyweight desktop client. And Neovim can replace a graphical text editor once you add the plugins you need.

Terminal is not as intimidating as it seems

Terminal has a reputation for being difficult because it greets you with a blank window and no obvious place to start. But you don’t need to learn the entire command line before you can use it. You can just start with a tool that does something useful, look up the few commands you need, and pick up the rest over time.
